strengths: Novel theoretical contribution connecting test-time scaling performance to verifier ROC curves, addressing gap in understanding imperfect verifiers (prior work focused on perfect verifiers via pass@N)

Rigorous mathematical analysis with sound proofs characterizing how early scaling (top-right ROC), final performance (ROC slope at origin), and extrapolation impossibility depend on different ROC properties
Strong de-emergence result (Proposition 3) providing important insight that large-scale performance cannot be predicted from small-scale without full ROC curve knowledge
Comprehensive theoretical coverage analyzing both rejection sampling and Best-of-N with low-compute and high-compute regime analysis, including surprising convergence result
Empirical validation across multiple generator-verifier pairs (Llama, Qwen) showing theoretical predictions match experiments with appropriate confidence intervals
Clear presentation of key insights through effective visualizations (Figures 1, 3) illustrating how different ROC curve regions matter for different scaling regimes
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: single benchmark (GSM8K), only 3 test questions in detail, selection bias toward 'hard' questions, no evaluation on domains with less reliable verifiers or subjective quality metrics, unclear generalization

Core theory-practice gap: Assumption 1 (absolutely continuous score distribution) violated in practice where verifiers output discrete scores; Appendix B workaround feels like a patch rather than principled solution; sensitivity to score discretization not analyzed

Incomplete method coverage: only analyzes simple resampling methods (RS, BoN), ignores reasoning-based methods acknowledged as 'prominently applied in industry'; restricted to binary correctness labels, doesn't handle continuous or partial correctness

Lacks practical guidance: no clear recommendation on when to use RS vs BoN given practical constraints (RS cannot be parallelized, requires threshold selection); unclear how to estimate T'(0), T'(1) from limited data in practice; no analysis of ROC curve estimation error impact

De-emergence result uses artificial ROC curve constructions (linear extensions, horizontal lines) whose empirical prevalence is unclear; lacks discussion of realistic scenarios where extrapolation fails

Insufficient intuition for key results: unclear why both methods converge to same limit T'(0)π/(T'(0)π+1-π); when T(0)=0 vs T(0)>0 and how common each case is not discussed; concavity assumption validity not explored

strengths: Novel and elegant theoretical characterization connecting test-time scaling performance to verifier ROC curves for both rejection sampling and Best-of-N methods
Rigorous mathematical treatment with sound proofs leveraging appropriate techniques (Taylor expansion, dominated convergence theorem, layer-cake formula)
Key insight that different compute regimes depend on different ROC curve regions - early scaling from top-right corner, final performance from slope at origin
Compelling result (Proposition 3) showing early-scale performance cannot predict large-scale performance due to ROC curve shape
Convergence theorem showing both methods reach same asymptotic accuracy is a surprising and unifying result
Clear presentation with good intuition before formal results; effective use of illustrative figures
Empirical predictions closely match observations across multiple generator-verifier pairs with tight confidence intervals
Thoughtful treatment of practical limitations (discrete scores via smoothing in Appendix B)
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: evaluation restricted to GSM8K (single domain) and only 3 specific test questions with selection bias toward difficult instances
Significant gap between theory and practice: assumes fixed independent generator/verifier, but real systems train them jointly with correlated samples
Theory only descriptive (given ROC, predict performance) rather than prescriptive - limited guidance on how to improve verifier quality for better scaling
No evaluation on reasoning-based methods which dominate recent applications; analysis limited to resampling approaches
Some theoretical results feel somewhat expected: Proposition 3 is intuitive given arbitrary ROC shapes; infinite-compute limits have unclear practical relevance
All verifiers from same model families (Qwen, Llama); no exploration of different verifier architectures or other scaling methods
Missing analysis of statistical estimation error and sensitivity to noise in empirical ROC curves
Assumption 1 violation (continuous scores) addressed via ad-hoc smoothing rather than principled approach
Limited actionable insights for practitioners - still requires empirical measurement of verifier ROC curves

strengths: Novel theoretical framework connecting test-time scaling to ROC curve geometry, providing elegant characterizations of RS and BoN methods
Rigorous mathematical analysis with complete proofs, including careful limit analysis using Taylor expansion and dominated convergence
Addresses practical problem of imperfect verifiers, well-motivated by systems like OpenAI's o1
Comprehensive theoretical contributions: local ROC properties determine early scaling (Prop 1), global properties determine limits (Prop 2), formal extrapolation impossibility (Props 3, 7)
Good experimental validation on GSM8K and MATH500 showing theoretical predictions match empirical results with multiple model combinations
Theoretical justification for RL connection (Prop 4) explaining why RS matches RL in certain limits
Thoughtful treatment of practical issues like discrete scores (Appendix E with smoothing argument)
weaknesses: Limited scope: only analyzes two simple resampling methods (RS, BoN); other test-time scaling approaches not covered; results may not generalize
Restrictive binary label assumption (y ∈ {0,1}) excludes partial credit and continuous quality metrics; extension to other settings unclear
Gap between theory and practice: results technically for fixed queries, ROC curves assumed known; unclear how to estimate from limited data and use predictions
Limited experimental breadth: only 2 math datasets, LLM-based verifiers only, generators up to 32B, per-instance experiments on few questions
Core insights feel somewhat expected (RS > BoN for fixed compute is intuitive; convergence at infinity is reasonable) despite elegant formalization
Lack of practical guidance: no recommendations for verifier design, threshold/N selection, or choosing between methods in realistic settings
Extrapolation impossibility results use adversarial ROC curve constructions—practical relevance unclear when verifiers follow natural patterns
No empirical validation that realistic verifier ROC curves satisfy concavity assumption used in key results (Props 1, 5, 6)
Missing ablations: no sensitivity analysis on generator accuracy π, different verifier training procedures, or generator-verifier family mismatches
Extension from fixed-query theory to aggregate dataset results (Figure 5) lacks rigorous justification; arbitrary RS compute cap (25) and null handling

strengths: Novel ROC curve framework elegantly characterizes test-time scaling performance by connecting local geometry to compute regimes
Rigorous mathematical contributions with non-trivial theorems on RS/BoN scaling behavior, limits, and impossibility of extrapolation
Strong empirical validation with per-instance predictions matching theory remarkably well across multiple model sizes and datasets
Addresses timely and practically relevant problem directly impacting modern LLM deployment strategies
Clear presentation with good intuition, comprehensive proofs, and thorough treatment of technical details including discrete score handling
Key insight that different ROC regions determine different compute regimes (T'(1) for low-compute, T'(0) for high-compute) is elegant and non-obvious
weaknesses: Limited theoretical scope: only two resampling methods analyzed; prominent test-time approaches (reasoning models, RL-based methods) lack analysis
Experiments confined to mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH500); generalization to other domains remains unclear
Practical applicability concerns: robust estimation of ROC curve (especially T'(0)) not addressed; no guidance for high-compute prediction without observation
No algorithmic contributions or improved methods proposed; paper is primarily characterization-focused rather than solution-oriented
Theory assumes fixed independent generator-verifier pair; doesn't address realistic scenarios of verifier fine-tuning on generator outputs
Missing analysis of sensitivity to generator accuracy π; most experiments use relatively low-accuracy generators
RL connection (Proposition 4) underdeveloped; no empirical comparison with practical RL-based scaling methods

strengths: Novel theoretical framework: ROC curve characterization of RS and BoN performance is elegant and provides genuine new insights into how verifier quality affects test-time scaling
Rigorous mathematical analysis: Complete characterization theorems (Propositions 1-2, Theorem 1) with detailed, apparently sound proofs covering both local and global scaling behavior
High-precision empirical validation: Theory predictions match empirical observations with remarkable accuracy (Figures 1, 4), validating per-instance predictions not just aggregates
Comprehensive treatment: Extensive analysis including low/high-compute regimes, impossibility results, practical algorithms (Capped RS), and RL connections
Practical insights despite theoretical focus: Identifies RS efficiency advantage (Proposition 6), proposes working hybrid method, shows importance of verifier quality across compute regimes
Clear presentation: Main contributions well-motivated with effective figures illustrating key insights
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Analyzes only existing methods (RS, BoN) without proposing fundamentally new test-time scaling approaches; Capped RS is a practical workaround rather than principled innovation

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: Critical dependence on ROC curve concavity, differentiability, and binary labels; limited guidance for non-concave cases; per-instance theory doesn't fully characterize aggregate behavior

Impossibility results limit practical utility: Propositions 3 and 7 show early performance cannot predict high-compute behavior, which is intellectually interesting but discouraging for practitioners without providing compensatory guidance

Limited experimental scope: Evaluation restricted to math and code domains with verifiable answers; missing comparison with other recent test-time scaling methods; no evaluation on open-ended tasks or domains with unreliable verifiers

Practical applicability gaps: No guidance on robust ROC curve estimation; difficulty-based threshold heuristic requires knowing query difficulty a priori; limited advice for practitioners choosing between RS and BoN

Incomplete analysis of realistic scenarios: Underexplores cases where generator and verifier are correlated; unclear how results extend to multi-step reasoning or tree-based methods; sensitivity to verifier architecture not addressed

strengths: Novel and elegant theoretical framework connecting test-time scaling performance to verifier ROC curves, providing precise characterization via Propositions 1-7 and Theorems 1-2
Important negative result (Propositions 3 and 7) rigorously establishing that high-compute performance cannot be predicted from low-compute observations, with careful construction of counterexamples
Solid experimental validation with per-instance predictions matching theory remarkably well (Figures 1, 4) across multiple models (Qwen, Llama) and datasets (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, HumanEval+)
Practical insights demonstrating RS outperforms BoN for fixed compute with concave ROC curves, and the development of practical hybrid methods (Capped RS) that work well in practice
Mathematically rigorous proofs using classical ML theory (ROC curves, concavity, dominated convergence) with comprehensive treatment of low-compute and high-compute regimes
Clear presentation with intuitive figures, comprehensive notation tables, and well-organized exposition balancing main text with detailed appendices
weaknesses: Limited methodological scope: analyzes only two simple methods (BoN, RS) with binary ground truth labels; limited engagement with increasingly prominent 'reasoning' methods (o1-style); RL connection (Proposition 4) only characterizes β→0 limit

Narrow experimental domain coverage: primarily mathematics problems (GSM8K, MATH500); verifiers only tested up to 32B scale; 1000 samples per question may be insufficient for accurate ROC curve estimation

Gap between theory and practice: theoretical results assume knowledge of exact ROC curves, but practice requires noisy estimation; aggregate results rely on ad-hoc heuristics for threshold selection (difficulty-based τ(q), capping)

Incomplete practical guidance: limited discussion on robustly estimating ROC curves with finite samples; missing analysis of verifier miscalibration effects; no guidance on how to choose thresholds in multi-verifier scenarios

Assumption limitations: Definition 1 assumes achieving any (TPR, FPR) tradeoff via thresholding which may not hold with quantized scores; limited discussion of tied scores handling; independence of samples assumption not explicitly justified

Presentation density: Many propositions presented with limited intuition beforehand; Figure 1 overlapping lines reduce readability; practical implications of some theoretical results could be highlighted more explicitly
